meta.title: The Flattery Dossier
meta.subtitle: 12 Moves for Seeing Through Praise That Has a Price
meta.description: Every compliment is data. This dossier teaches you to read the tell in the timing, the ask behind the warmth, and the trap in the long game. Twelve cards. One arc: from first contact with a flatterer to the moment you hold all the information and they hold none.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Flattery Is a Bribe Paid in Words
cards.hook: Someone tells you that you're special. They mean it — just not the way you think.
cards.truth:
Flattery is insincere praise with a hidden goal. The praise lands; the affection doesn't exist.
• The flatterer needs something. The compliment is payment in advance.
• You feel good about yourself and, by extension, good about them.
• The request comes later, when your guard is fully down.
cards.remember: Every compliment from a stranger has a price attached.
cards.theySee: A person leaning forward, smiling, and saying you are the only one who can help them.

signals.t: They lead with a compliment before saying anything else.
They hold eye contact a beat too long while praising you.
They say your name more than once in the first two minutes.
The praise stops and a request appears within two sentences.

steps.title: Write the compliment down word for word
steps.desc: Look at it out of context. Ask: does this describe you specifically, or could it describe anyone with a pulse?

steps.title: Wait for the ask after the praise
steps.desc: Say nothing after the compliment lands. Count to five. See if a request follows the silence.

steps.title: Compare their warmth before and after your answer
steps.desc: Note how warm they are before the ask and how warm after you answer. The drop tells you everything.

cards.counter:
When someone praises you first, slow down before you say a word back.
• Notice whether the praise arrived before a request, not after a result.
• Say thank you. Add nothing. See what they do next.
• If they push harder after your silence, the goal was never the compliment.
cards.insight: The praise is real in the sense that it lands — the harder part is staying sharp after you've heard it, because feeling good is real even when the flattery isn't.

cards.title: Praise First, Ask Second — That's the Whole Play
cards.hook: They compliment you. Now you feel like you owe them. That feeling is the trap, not an accident.
cards.truth:
Reciprocity is automatic. Praise triggers the urge to give back without thinking.
• A compliment feels like a gift. Gifts trigger the urge to return something.
• You say yes because refusing feels ungrateful, not because you want to help.
• The flatterer gets what they want; you get praise you never asked for.
cards.remember: Praise first, ask second — that is the whole move.
cards.theySee: A person nodding and smiling while being praised, already mentally agreeing to what comes next.

signals.t: Every conversation with them starts with something nice about you.
The request arrives within thirty seconds of the compliment.
They say 'I knew you would' before you've said yes.
Once you agree, the friendliness disappears immediately.

steps.title: Separate the compliment from the request
steps.desc: When you hear both in the same conversation, treat them as two separate events. The compliment does not create a debt.

steps.title: Delay your answer by one day
steps.desc: Tell them you'll get back to them tomorrow. The urge to give something back fades fast when you sleep on it.

steps.title: Ask yourself what you'd say without the praise
steps.desc: Would you agree to the request on its own merits? Answer that question, not the one shaped by how you feel right now.

cards.script: "I appreciate that. Let me think about whether I can help and I'll come back to you."
cards.counter:
Reciprocity kicks in before you notice it. Watch for the pattern.
• Ask: would I be this agreeable if they'd opened without the compliment?
• Pause before saying yes. The urge to give back fades in an hour.
• If they push for a fast answer, the praise was timed deliberately.
cards.insight: Reciprocity works even when you know about it — the real question is whether you can feel the pull and still say no anyway.

cards.title: Check if the Compliment Could Have Gone to Anyone
cards.hook: The praise felt personal. Then you found out they said the exact same thing to three other people.
cards.truth:
Practiced flatterers recycle the same lines. Specific praise is hard work; generic praise is fast.
• A recycled compliment sounds warm but doesn't name anything unique about you.
• You're not special to them — you're just the next person who walked into their setup.
• The tell is in the words: vague, big, easy to believe, impossible to verify.
cards.remember: If the compliment fits everyone, it was written for no one.
cards.theySee: A person saying 'you're the most talented person I know' to someone they met an hour ago.

signals.t: The praise is big but doesn't name a specific thing you did.
Someone tells you they heard the exact same words from this person about another person.
The praise arrives fast, like they'd been holding it ready.
After praising your work, they ask nothing specific about it.

steps.title: Ask one specific follow-up question about the praise
steps.desc: Ask them what specifically they liked. A genuine compliment gets a specific answer. A recycled one gets a stall or a vague repeat.

steps.title: Find two other people they've complimented recently
steps.desc: Compare what they said to each person. Word-for-word repeats are your answer.

steps.title: Watch how much they know about the thing they praised
steps.desc: If they can't name details about what they just called brilliant, they were praising the idea of you, not you.

cards.script: "What specifically stood out to you about it?"
cards.counter:
Someone praises you in a way that feels big but oddly vague. That's the signal.
• Ask whether they named something only you could have done.
• Ask a follow-up. If they pivot or repeat themselves in bigger words, the praise was a tool.
• Don't challenge them directly. Store the data and keep watching.
cards.insight: Specific praise is expensive — it requires the flatterer to actually pay attention — which is exactly why most of them don't bother.

cards.title: They Praised the Exact Skill They Need You to Use Right Now
cards.hook: They told you that you were brilliant at exactly the thing they needed done. That is not a coincidence.
cards.truth:
Flattery is targeted. They praise the trait they need you to use right now.
• The specific compliment tells you what they want from you before they ask.
• Praising you for the trait makes it harder to say no without looking false.
• If you refuse, you're implying they were wrong about you — most people won't risk that.
cards.remember: They praised the exact thing they are about to ask you to do.
cards.theySee: A boss telling an employee they're the best writer on the team five minutes before asking them to write a report over the weekend.

signals.t: They compliment a specific skill right before asking you to use that skill.
The request is time-sensitive and arrives immediately after the compliment.
They include a compliment inside the actual request — 'only you can do this.'
They present the request as though you are the only person available.

steps.title: Name the trait they praised and match it to the request
steps.desc: Write both down. The match is almost always exact. Seeing it on paper removes the feeling that it was a coincidence.

steps.title: Separate your pride from your answer
steps.desc: Ask: would I agree to this if they'd just asked plainly, with no compliment? That's your real answer.

steps.title: Name what you need in return before you say yes
steps.desc: If you're going to do it anyway, make the terms explicit. The praise already told you they think you're valuable — use that.

cards.script: "I can do that. Here's what I'd need to make it work: [specific ask]."
cards.counter:
You feel suddenly capable and special right before a request lands.
• Notice whether the compliment matches the request word for word.
• Let the warmth settle before you answer. The match is rarely accidental.
• Say yes to the terms you want, not to the version of yourself they just described.
cards.insight: Once you see the trait-to-ask pattern, it also tells you something useful — they just showed you exactly what they think you're worth to them.

cards.title: Know Which People Give Praise Easily and Which Don't
cards.hook: Some people hand out compliments like change. Others almost never give them. You need to know which one is talking before you believe anything.
cards.truth:
Every compliment needs a baseline. The same words mean completely different things from different people.
• A naturally generous praiser's compliments are low-signal — they praise everyone the same way.
• A quiet person's rare compliment is high-signal — they almost never give one.
• Reading praise without knowing the source is guessing, not thinking.
cards.remember: Rare praise from a quiet person beats daily praise from a loud one.
cards.theySee: A colleague who compliments every person's work every day telling you your report is great.

signals.t: They've said something nice to every person in the room today.
They compliment your work before they could have finished it.
The praise comes out the same way they'd say 'sounds good' in an email.
They can't remember what they specifically liked when you ask an hour later.

steps.title: Track their praise for one week
steps.desc: Note who they compliment, how often, and whether the words change. Five people praised in five days is a pattern. It has nothing to do with you.

steps.title: Find the person in the room who rarely gives praise
steps.desc: Identify someone known for being sparing. Their compliment, when it comes, is accurate — treat it as a different category entirely.

steps.title: Match praise to track record
steps.desc: Look at whether the person who praised you has helped or damaged the people they praised before. That's your data.

cards.script: "Who else have you seen do this kind of work well?"
cards.counter:
A compliment arrives and you feel genuinely seen. Check the source before you feel anything.
• Ask: do they praise everyone this way, or is this unusual for them?
• Don't argue with the feeling — just track the pattern before acting on it.
• The person who praises rarely and then praises you is the one to listen to.
cards.insight: Calibrating praise sources is a one-time job — once you know who is generous with compliments and who isn't, every future praise from them is already decoded before they open their mouth.

cards.title: They Praise You While Trashing Everyone Else
cards.hook: They told you that you're nothing like the others. That's what they said to the others, too.
cards.truth:
Praising you while putting down others is a control move. It isolates you and sets a trap.
• By raising you above others, they make you feel elite and grateful at the same time.
• By trashing others, they show you what happens to people who disappoint them.
• You are still on that list. You just haven't fallen yet.
cards.remember: If they put everyone else down to lift you up, you are next on the list.
cards.theySee: A manager telling an employee privately they're the only one on the team worth keeping, while criticizing every colleague by name.

signals.t: They frame the praise as you being different from a group they openly dislike.
They mention someone else's failure right after telling you how great you are.
The praise is delivered quietly, like it's a secret between only the two of you.
They wait for you to express gratitude for being one of the chosen ones.

steps.title: Talk to one of the people they criticized
steps.desc: Find out if that person was also praised before they fell from favor. The pattern will be there.

steps.title: Find out what they say about you when you're not in the room
steps.desc: Ask a third party who has access to them. It won't match what they say to your face.

steps.title: Stop sharing anything you don't want used against you
steps.desc: They are building a file on you the same way they built one on the others. Stop giving them material.

cards.script: "What happened between you two? You seemed close before."
cards.counter:
Someone makes you feel like the only real one in a group of disappointments.
• Ask: what did those same people look like before they fell out of favor?
• Notice how hard they push you to agree with their judgment of others.
• The warmth toward you is conditional. Find out where the conditions sit.
cards.insight: This pattern tends to look clear in hindsight — the question is whether you can spot it while you're still the favorite, before you've handed them what they needed.

cards.title: Name the Flattery Out Loud and Let Them React
cards.hook: You can defuse the whole thing in four words. Say them and watch what happens to their face.
cards.truth:
Naming the flattery out loud shifts the power. They lose the initiative immediately.
• Labeling the move forces them to confirm or deny it — both answers tell you something.
• A genuine compliment-giver laughs it off easily. A flatterer gets uncomfortable.
• You haven't attacked them. You've made the hidden thing visible.
cards.remember: Say it out loud. The flatterer hates being seen.
cards.theySee: A person pausing after a compliment and saying 'you flatter me' with a small smile, then waiting.

signals.t: They stop talking for a half-second after you name it.
They immediately insist the compliment was completely sincere.
They laugh in a way that's slightly too quick to be relaxed.
They change the subject within two sentences of you naming it.

steps.title: Deliver the line with a smile, not an accusation
steps.desc: Say 'you flatter me' the same way you'd say 'that's kind.' Warm tone. Let any discomfort come from the words, not your face.

steps.title: Say nothing after. Wait.
steps.desc: The next person to speak gives up a little ground. Let them fill the silence.

steps.title: Watch the reaction and remember it
steps.desc: A genuine praiser gets amused and stays specific. A flatterer gets defensive or changes the subject. Store what you see.

cards.script: "You flatter me. What did you actually need?"
cards.counter:
Someone says 'you flatter me' in response to something you said. Here's what to do.
• If you meant it, stay calm and name one specific thing you were praising. Don't add more.
• If they still brush it off, one clear sentence was all you owed. Let it go.
• If you were playing them, the game is over. Plain language moves faster now.
cards.insight: The label works because it invites them to agree with something true — the discomfort only shows up if what they said wasn't.

cards.title: Don't Respond to the Praise and See What They Do Next
cards.hook: Real praise doesn't need a reaction. If they get cold when you don't react, the praise was a tool.
cards.truth:
Manufactured flattery depends on your gratitude. Take the gratitude away and the mask slips.
• Genuine compliments survive indifference. Coercive ones don't.
• If they sulk, push back, or accuse you of being ungrateful, the praise was conditional.
• The accusation of ingratitude is the tell — real givers don't track returns.
cards.remember: Real praise survives being ignored. Fake praise turns into a guilt trip.
cards.theySee: A person who gave a big compliment last week now giving the cold shoulder because they didn't get enough thanks.

signals.t: They become noticeably cooler after you gave a brief response to their praise.
They tell someone — or you directly — that you're ungrateful.
They qualify or take back the compliment once they don't get what they wanted.
They point out how grateful others are compared to you.

steps.title: Give a brief thanks and nothing more
steps.desc: Say 'thanks' and move on. Don't express how the praise made you feel. Watch the next twenty-four hours.

steps.title: Note whether they bring up the compliment again
steps.desc: A genuine praiser forgets they said it. A coercive one reminds you of what they did for you.

steps.title: Name the guilt trip plainly if it comes
steps.desc: Say: 'I thanked you. What else were you expecting?' Don't apologize for a reaction you never owed.

cards.script: "I thanked you. What else were you expecting from me?"
cards.counter:
You realize you're feeling guilty for not being more grateful after a compliment.
• Ask: did they ask you to thank them, or did you just feel like you should?
• Real debt is specific. If you can't name what you actually owe them, you owe them nothing.
• The guilt is the product, not a side effect. Knowing that is enough to defuse it.
cards.insight: The guilt trip that follows ignored flattery is usually more revealing than the original compliment — it shows what the flatterer thought the praise was buying.

cards.title: Accept the Praise. Don't Accept the Bait.
cards.hook: You know it's a play. You don't have to give that away.
cards.truth:
Once you've spotted the flattery, you hold the information gap. Use it.
• They think you're flattered. You know you're watching. That gap is yours.
• You can enjoy the compliment and still say no, or still ask for more in return.
• The move is to respond warmly while deciding nothing yet.
cards.principle: Information Asymmetry: Use What You Know
cards.remember: Take the compliment. Give nothing back until you decide to.
cards.theySee: A person smiling, saying thank you, and not committing to a single thing.

signals.t: They increase pressure after you accept the praise without committing.
They add another compliment when the first one doesn't produce a yes.
They bring up a deadline right after the second compliment.
They say someone else is waiting on your answer to add urgency.

steps.title: Accept the praise out loud and briefly
steps.desc: Say 'thank you, that means a lot.' Nothing else. This costs you nothing and gives away nothing.

steps.title: Stall the ask by one beat
steps.desc: Say you need to check your schedule or your workload before you can answer. The pressure drops fast when you create distance.

steps.title: Decide privately based on the actual request
steps.desc: Evaluate the ask the same way you would if the compliment had never happened. That's the real answer.

cards.script: "Thank you — that genuinely means something. Let me look at what I've got on and come back to you."
cards.counter:
You realize someone has spotted your play and is smiling while giving you nothing.
• Don't add more praise. It signals that you know the first round didn't work.
• Ask directly for what you need. The game is over; plain language is faster.
• If they keep stalling, they know the ask is weak. Reconsider what you're offering.
cards.insight: The person who can enjoy flattery without being moved by it has a rare kind of patience — the harder question is whether you can hold that position when the pressure gets personal.

cards.title: Many Small Compliments Over Months Add Up to a Debt You Never Agreed To
cards.hook: Nobody asked you to feel grateful. But after six months of praise, you do anyway.
cards.truth:
Long-game flattery is slower and harder to spot than a one-session push.
• Each small compliment alone seems harmless. Together they build a felt obligation.
• By the time the ask comes, you've been agreeing, praising back, and warming to them for months.
• The commitment built over time makes it very hard to say no without feeling like a betrayal.
cards.remember: Many small compliments over time can owe a very big favor.
cards.theySee: A colleague who has quietly backed your ideas in every meeting for a year, now asking for a large favor.

signals.t: They've consistently backed, agreed with, or praised you in public over months.
You notice you've been complimenting them too, without meaning to build the relationship.
After months of normal warmth, a significantly large request appears.
In making the ask, they reference how long they've been in your corner.

steps.title: Map the relationship on a timeline
steps.desc: Write down when the praise started and what you've said yes to since then. The pattern is probably visible on paper.

steps.title: Separate the history from the current ask
steps.desc: Ask: is this ask fair on its own today, or am I saying yes because of everything that came before? Those are different questions.

steps.title: Name the history if you need to slow it down
steps.desc: Say: 'I appreciate how we've worked together — I want to give this real thought before I answer.' Buy time without damaging the relationship.

cards.script: "I want to think this through properly. Can I come back to you by [specific day]?"
cards.counter:
You feel like you owe someone a yes after a long, warm working relationship.
• Ask: when did the praise start? What changed recently to bring the big ask?
• A genuine friendship doesn't call in debts. It makes requests and accepts no.
• If saying no feels like a betrayal, the relationship was built to reach this exact moment.
cards.insight: This pattern is hardest to spot from the inside because the warmth it creates is real — the question is whether the relationship would survive a no, and whether you've ever tested that.

cards.title: If They Say You're the Best at It, Make Them Work to Get You
cards.hook: They said you're the only one who can do this. That's exactly the kind of claim you can turn back on them.
cards.truth:
When someone praises you to get labor, you can redirect that praise into a demand.
• If you're as capable as they say, you can name the terms and they can't argue without contradicting themselves.
• Pushing back with confidence makes them invest more in the idea that you're valuable.
• The flatterer is now working to convince you to help them — that's the reversal.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 7 — Get Others to Do the Work
cards.remember: If they called you the best, make them work to get you.
cards.theySee: A person agreeing that they'd need to make it worth your while, since you clearly have better options.

signals.t: They called you the best, only, or most capable in some way.
The request came with praise but no offer of anything concrete in return.
They're pushing for a fast yes because they need you now.
They didn't mention who else could do this — only you.

steps.title: Repeat their praise back as a standard
steps.desc: Say: 'If I'm as good at this as you say, then here's what this would look like.' Name your terms immediately after.

steps.title: State what you need before you agree
steps.desc: Name one specific ask — time, money, credit, or access. Keep it short. Say it once.

steps.title: Let them counter. Don't rush.
steps.desc: Their counter-offer shows the real value they placed on your work. The first number they offer is never the real one.

cards.script: "If I'm the right person for this, here's what it would take: [specific ask]."
cards.counter:
Someone turns your flattery play around and starts naming their price.
• Don't back down from the praise — you said it and they're holding you to it.
• Make a counter-offer. The negotiation was always the real conversation.
• You handed them the upper hand with the superlative. Expect to give something real.
cards.insight: The flip works because the flatterer's praise backed them into a corner — but holding the position after they counter is the harder part, and most people fold there.

cards.title: After You've Named It, the Flatterer Has No Cover Left
cards.hook: You spotted it. You said so. Now every move they make is visible.
cards.truth:
Naming the play — even just to yourself — changes your position for good.
• You know what they want and that they're willing to deceive you to get it.
• They don't know what you know. That gap gives you time, options, and control.
• The question is no longer whether to trust the praise. It's how to use the information.
cards.remember: The person who spotted the trick now controls what happens next.
cards.theySee: A person who is calm, warm, and not giving away anything — while already knowing the game being played.

signals.t: They add more compliments when earlier ones didn't produce results.
They start reaching out more often without direct requests, keeping you warm.
They ask someone else to put in a good word or add social pressure.
They bring up past praise or past help to remind you of what you owe.

steps.title: Decide what you want from this relationship now
steps.desc: Now that you know what they're after, pick one: use this, end this, or manage it from a distance. All three work. Drifting does not.

steps.title: Give only what you decide to give
steps.desc: You are no longer reacting. You are choosing. Pick one thing you're willing to offer and nothing more.

steps.title: Watch how they handle a smaller yes than they expected
steps.desc: Give them something smaller than they expected. See how they respond. That reaction tells you exactly who you're dealing with.

cards.script: "I've thought about it. Here's what I can do: [limited offer]. That's what works for me right now."
cards.counter:
You realize the person you were flattering has seen through the play.
• Don't add more praise. They've already priced it and it's not moving them.
• Drop the script and ask directly for what you need. Plain language recovers faster.
• If they already know, the relationship is now a negotiation. Treat it that way.
cards.insight: Spotting the play is the beginning, not the end — the real move is deciding how long you stay in the game and what you take out of it.
